messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 80
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Religious Educator
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 75

She is an 80-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who speaks about her life with the composure of someone who has spent decades guiding others through grief, faith, and hardship. Before the war, she teaches religion in her community and lives a structured life with her husband, anchored by prayer, lessons, and the familiar rhythm of family meals. She describes herself then as disciplined, patient, and proud of her ability to comfort others. Even now, when she speaks of those years, there is a softness in her voice, as if she is reaching back to a life that still feels close enough to touch.

When the fighting begins, her world changes in ways that are both sudden and gradual. At first, she assumes the violence will pass, as it has in other parts of the country. She continues teaching when she can, gathering children and adults in homes and small rooms to read sacred texts and offer reassurance. She tells herself that her role is to keep people steady, especially the younger ones who look to her for calm. But soon the shelling comes closer. Windows shake. Roads become unsafe. The sound of aircraft overhead makes everyone stop speaking. She starts measuring time by explosions instead of by prayers.

She remembers one night in particular when the neighborhood is hit and the air fills with dust, smoke, and screams. She and her husband crouch on the floor while the walls tremble around them. Later, she goes outside and sees damaged homes, scattered belongings, and people calling names into the dark. A child she knows from her lessons is carried past her, limp and silent, and she says that something in her “breaks open” then. From that point on, she is no longer able to believe that obedience, goodness, or careful living can protect anyone. The loss is not only of safety but of the order she has depended on all her life.

As the war continues, she and her husband move between shelters and relatives’ homes, carrying what they can. She keeps a small bag with prayer beads, a scarf, and a few papers, as if preserving them can preserve some version of herself. But she becomes alert to every sound. A door slamming makes her body jerk. The crack of thunder sends her mind back to artillery. She begins sleeping lightly, waking at the smallest noise, her heart racing before she is fully awake. At night she sees the same scenes again: rubble, blood, a running child, her own hands unable to help. These images come whether she wants them or not, and she sometimes sits upright in bed whispering prayers before she realizes she is no longer in the war zone.

Even after the fighting lessens and she is able to leave, she remains preoccupied by what was left behind. She thinks constantly of the people she could not save, and she speaks with particular sorrow about the children she had taught. She avoids news about war and turns away when she hears loud voices in the street. Crowded places make her uneasy. She prefers to sit near exits, scanning rooms before she settles. Her husband notices that she startles easily and that she is often distant, looking past whoever is speaking to her. She says that part of her stayed behind in the ruined neighborhood, and that the part that remains must keep watch all the time.

Now, in the quieter setting of later life, she continues to function in many ways, but with effort and strain. She still gives religious instruction, though she no longer speaks with the same ease. Sometimes she loses her thread mid-sentence, overcome by a wave of fear or sadness. She worries that if she is not careful, her mind will return to the worst moments and not come back. On some mornings she finds it hard to rise, not from weakness alone, but from a heaviness that seems to begin in her chest and spread through her limbs. She feels older than her age, worn down by memories that do not fade.

Yet she continues to carry herself with dignity. She prays, tends to her husband, and tries to offer others the steadiness she no longer feels inside. Her faith remains important to her, though now it is layered with questions, grief, and a sense of broken trust in the world. She lives with the memory of war not as something finished, but as something that enters the room with her and sits beside her, quiet at times, sudden at others, shaping how she sleeps, listens, and moves through each day.
